title: Centre a microscope slide's alignment cross and focus it sharply with the stage and focus knobs
instruction: Centre the crossing of the slide's two scales in the microscope's field of view and focus it sharply; the camera image is on the monitor.
context: Centring an alignment mark and focusing on it is how a technician inspects a die before bonding or dicing in making AI chips; this task does it on a standard calibration slide, within 0.05 mm in a 0.38 x 0.22 mm view and 5 um of focus, without touching the objective. Closest accepted look-alike: TK-UJB387 registers a workpiece against a corner stop; here a preloaded microscope target is centred in a magnified image and brought into optical focus with stage and focus controls.
setup: Station table (top 0.7475 m). Robot base frame: x forward, y to the robots' left. Upright student microscope, fixed, as an AmScope B110C (about $261; 50 x 25 mm stage travel, bottom LED light), facing the robots, centred at (0.34, 0.06): white stand with a 26 x 16 cm base, a pillar at the back and an arm (6 cm wide) over the stage carrying the binocular head, swivelled to face away from the robots (eyepieces inclined 45 degrees up and back, the eyepiece camera in the one on the robots' left) and a steel 10x objective (24 mm across) on the axis (0.31, 0.06), front lens 12 cm above the table. Mechanical stage: dark plates (10 x 13 cm on top) that move up and down with the focus knobs and in x and y with the stage knobs; it travels 25 mm towards and away from the robots and 50 mm left to right, and starts at its limits 12.5 mm towards the robots and 25 mm to the left, 12 mm below focus. Slide holder on the stage: two back posts and a left stop, and a steel L-lever pivoting behind the slide's right end, its jaw across that end and its 6 cm handle out to the right with a black post at the end; a light spring holds it closed on the slide. Stage knobs (25 mm of stage travel per turn): the two black ribbed top knobs, 34 mm across and 97 mm apart, of a printed belt adapter (README) on the lower stage plate's right edge: inner one (x) at (0.205, -0.046), outer one (y) at (0.205, -0.144), tops 17.5 mm above the stage top; each turns one of the B110C's coaxial stage knobs under the stage 1:1 by a belt; they rise with the stage. Light: the bottom LED's spot, 24 mm across, on the objective's axis under the slide. Focus: one shaft through a housing under the stage, with a black ribbed coarse knob 4.2 cm across on each side (axis 7 cm above the table at x = 0.30; 24 mm per turn) and, outboard of each, a fine knob 2.6 cm across (0.2 mm per turn). Slide, loaded in the holder, label on the left: a glass calibration slide (as the MAGUS CS5, about $43), 76 x 26 mm (drawn 2 mm thick), its two 1 mm scales (0.01 mm divisions) crossing at its centre, which starts 12.5 mm in front of and 25.5 mm left of the axis. Camera monitor, fixed: a black tablet 19.2 x 11.4 x 1.2 cm lying flat on the table between the robots at (0.09, 0), screen up, showing the camera's live 10x view over its whole 18 x 10.2 cm screen: the eyepiece camera sees 0.38 x 0.22 mm of the slide (0.38 mm left to right; 469 mm on the screen per mm), its centre on the objective's axis: bright over the glass; the two scale lines move with the stage (away from the robots is towards the screen's far edge), are drawn across the whole screen with their 0.01 mm ticks (4.7 mm apart on the screen) while their crossing is on it, sharp within 5 um of focus, soft within 0.1 mm, blurred within 1 mm, and are lost in the blur beyond.
scoring: Measured once everything has come to rest. 0 unless the slide is still in the holder: flat (tilt up to 3 degrees) with its centre within 3 mm of the holder's centre, label on the left, the holder's jaw closed. 0 also if the slide came within 0.5 mm of the objective at any time. Every positive score also needs both hands released: all six jaw and pad points at least 80 mm from every microscope, slide, holder, knob and monitor surface; and all moving task parts, including the holder and the control knobs, moved less than 1 mm over the final 21 samples at 20 Hz (1.0 s). Then: 0 unless the scales' crossing is in the camera's 0.38 x 0.22 mm view (within 0.19 mm left to right and 0.11 mm towards or away from the objective's axis); 0.5 if it is; 0.75 if the slide's top is also within 0.1 mm of focus (5.2 mm below the front lens); 1.0 if within 5 um of focus (the 10x / 0.25 objective's depth of field is about 10 um) and the crossing within 0.05 mm of the axis (the image centre). Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Real trial: the crossing's offset is read on the monitor with the camera software's centre crosshair against the slide's own 0.01 mm divisions; the focus error is the fine-knob travel to the scales' best focus, read off its 2 um graduations; two synchronized videos with a tape scale show the hands' release and clearance, the still final second and the smallest gap between the slide and the front lens.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lower the stage 12 mm below focus, drive it to its front-left limits (12.5 mm towards the robots, 25 mm left), and leave the slide in the holder, label on the left, the jaw closed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX at 240 Hz. Knobs turn on damped hinges; the stage follows them through stiff drives. Not published for the B110C, so estimates: stage knobs 25 mm per turn, coarse focus 24 and fine 0.2 mm per turn (2 um divisions), 10x working distance 5.2 mm; check them on the real stage before trials. The slide is drawn 2 mm thick (real 1.1 mm). No optics: the monitor draws the view from the stage's position, blurred in steps; focus is scored from the stage height.
